alignment.note: Greek uses an aorist participle (ἐξελθόντες, 'having gone out'); the Vulgate matches with a present participle (exeuntes); the Peshitta renders the verb finitely with ܘܢܦܩܘ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܘ, a typical Syriac periphrastic construction expressing past durative or narrative aspect rather than subordination.

Greek and Peshitta use the aorist/perfect ('they proclaimed', ἐκήρυξαν / ܘܐܟܪܙܘ); the Vulgate prefers the imperfect prædicabant, conveying ongoing or iterative preaching, a stylistic tense shift common in the Latin gospel tradition.

Greek expresses repentance with a single verb (μετανοῶσιν) and Syriac likewise with one finite verb (ܕܢܬܘܒܘܢ, from the root meaning 'to turn/return'); the Vulgate uses the periphrastic idiom pœnitentiam agerent ('that they might do penance'), an analytic construction that later carried significant theological weight in Western penitential doctrine.

The Greek transmits a comma after μετανοῶσιν while the Vulgate closes the clause with a colon; the Peshitta as given carries no terminal punctuation. These are editorial divisions and do not affect the sense.
